prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in such moire systems

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene has the structure I value most in a physics prize: a precise theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011, flat bands at a magic angle) followed by an experiment in which nature realised it, with correlated insulators and superconductivity found in 2018 and then reproduced in many independent laboratories and extended to other moire platforms. It created a new field, tunable moire quantum matter, rather than refining an existing one. Having read the openings, I am moving B005 to the top of my own list. It is the only candidate that is ranked first or second by four members and appears in the top four of all eight ballots, so the committee's judgement of its importance does not depend on one subfield's tastes. This is a change from my opening view, in which I ranked anyonic statistics (B001) first. I still regard B001 as the most conceptually elegant case, but I cannot claim that a candidate with three supporters and an unsettled experimental credit chain is the best use of the prize this year when B005 offers theory plus discovery with a defensible three-person split.
statement.case_against: The microscopic origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated states is still debated, so the interpretation of the central phenomenon is not settled, and the prize would be given for the existence and tunability of the phenomena and for the flat-band prediction rather than for an understood mechanism. The field is also young and fast moving, and the credit chain has a visible gap: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 experiments, is not among the credited names, and earlier theoretical work on twisted layers (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto and others) as well as the broader moire experiments (for example Dean and Young) could be argued to deserve mention. A three-person prize cannot resolve all of this, and a citation worded too narrowly could read as unfair.

responses.point: Pearce ranks optical lattice clocks (B007) first as a genuine instrument breakthrough with quantitative, repeated confirmation at the 1e-18 level, and flags the omission of Yuan Cao from the twisted bilayer graphene credit as a real attribution concern.
responses.response: I agree that the Cao omission is the most serious attribution reservation against B005, and I would treat it as a reason to word the citation around the discovery of the phenomena by the Jarillo-Herrero group and the prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald, not to dismiss the case. The Statutes allow at most three names, and a junior first author left out of a three-person prize is regrettable but is a recurrent feature of the prize, not a scientific disqualification. On B007, I accept the instrument-breakthrough argument and the clean two-person attribution, which is a real advantage. My difference is one of kind: the clocks are an extraordinary refinement of a measurement we already knew how to make, whereas B005 opened a regime of matter that was not on the map. I would not be unhappy to see B007 awarded, which is why I list it as the first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B005 first, arguing that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction plus the 2018 observations form a conceptually clean and original theory-and-experiment pair that opened twistronics, with timing that is already appropriate.
responses.response: I largely agree and this is the main reason I moved. Where I would qualify Eriksson's framing is on maturity: calling the flat-band and correlated-insulator phenomenology well established is right, but the claim that recognition is timely should not slide into treating the superconducting mechanism as understood. I would keep the citation to the prediction and the observation of the phenomena, and avoid any wording that implies a settled explanation of the pairing. I also think Eriksson's three-name configuration with Bistritzer is better justified than a two-name one, because the prediction is a joint result and the model's authorship is not separable.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B007 first and atom interferometry (B043) second as precision measurement at its most fundamental, and sees B005 as important and original but 'somewhat early but defensible' because the pairing interpretation is not stable.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously and it is my own largest worry, but I disagree that it should push B005 behind the metrology candidates. Eight years of replication across many groups, spectroscopy and microscopy supporting the flat-band picture, and extension to other moire systems seem to me enough for the discovery itself, which is what the prize would reward. I also resist B043 as a companion or substitute: Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich are a plausible attribution, but Chu's earlier prize for laser cooling and the three-way split of the interferometer credit make it a weaker case than B007 within the same measurement theme, and only three members rank it at all.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the hexatic melting candidate (B025) first as a clean, original and lasting statistical-physics idea that extends the topological-defect picture, while placing B005 third with some concern that recognition could be slightly early.
responses.response: B025 is a beautiful and mature idea and I understand the appeal, but I find it difficult to place it ahead of B005 this year. It rests on the same defect-unbinding picture already honoured in 2016 and the transition order remains debated across systems, and it has support from only one ballot. Mehlig's concern that B005 could be slightly early deserves weight, but the three-person structure Mehlig himself would reduce to two names (leaving out Bistritzer) seems to me the weaker choice, since the 2011 prediction is a joint contribution of the model's authors in the sense that matters for credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a prize whose central superconducting phenomenon lacks an agreed mechanism, or will judge the field slightly early.
How to treat Yuan Cao and earlier twisted-bilayer theory under the three-person limit; the supplied credited names do not include them.

Whether B001 should be preferred after all if colleagues can resolve the experimental credit (Heiblum, Fève, Manfra, Rosenow) and the 2020 interferometer interpretation; I have not verified details beyond memory.
Whether a metrology prize (B007) would be seen as more secure on maturity and attribution, and so should take precedence this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My professional connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not appear among the credited names of any shortlisted candidate, and my own research in string theory, de Sitter space and cosmology is not close to the shortlisted topics.
